en: May they perish! They will make you crawl.
If you go as a hostage, they will do you no good;
My brother, in the end they will not leave you unharmed.
They have bozo poured into a camel-hide bucket;
In the house of the smiling Sart,
There is something deadly mixed with it.
Do not grow drunk on their bozo;
My brother, do not fall into a needless affliction!
In that accursed Sart's house,
There is bozo brewed from rice;
Burning poison is mixed within it.
Do not grow drunk on their bozo;
Little brother, do not meet your death this way!
Alty-Shaar is no land for you;
Those Sarts are no people of yours.
Kokand is no land for you;
Those hunched dogs are no people of yours.
Deceit lies in their eyes;
If those old wretches can,
They mean to bring you down.
Crookedness lies within them;
Falsehood lies in their words.
If they find their chance, little brother,
They mean to do for you.
If you go as a hostage, they will do you no good;
In the end they will not leave you unharmed.
All the Sarts have sworn an oath,
Have made their promise firm:
To trick you into becoming a hostage,
To offer you as a sacrifice,
To remove you from this world,
To finish you off,
To cut off your head and tie it up,
And receive repeated rewards for the good news.
You have many enemies facing you
To whom they can bring the glad tidings.
Countless treasures, riches and gold
They mean to take as their share of booty.
They chewed white wheat flour;
They held the Holy Quran.
They made their promise firm;
To slaughter you outright,
They swore an oath unto death.'
Then, speaking these words,
She now burst into piercing tears;
Her only one, gained through mortal hardship,
She now sent toward Bukhara.
He rode toward Bukhara, stirred to action,
Furious and carried away,
Finding no mountain to hurl himself against,
Finding no foe to fight,
Finding no embers to walk through,
Finding no bullet to meet,
Finding no road from which none returns,
To encounter and do battle,
Finding no full thousand troops.
The banner fluttered in his hand;
The white jacket with golden collar
Gleamed upon his shoulders.
The hearts of those who saw him were stirred;
Every limb, his majesty,
Seemed just like his father's.
Stretching like a lion,
Impatient with the journey,
He took the road toward Bukhara.
When the boy drew near,
God set him a trial:
Coming straight toward him he met
A dervish riding a gray bull.
A white turban was on his head;
He himself was ninety years old.
His appearance differed from other men's;
Every limb was utterly unlike theirs;
He had the awe of a saint.
When he saw the dervish,
His heart was deeply moved;
The dervish standing there
Seemed greater even than his father.
He now leaped down from his steed;
The white lead-rope braided in the okoro manner
He laid snugly round his neck.
Both hands upon his breast,
He pleaded with the dervish:
'Gladden this restless soul;
Be a blessing to me, dervish.
To a helpless one like me,
Be a father, dervish.
See that I am but a child;
You who resemble a prophet, O father,
Give me a good blessing before you go!
Father dervish, if I hunger, feed me;
If I grow thin, fatten me;
If I lose my way, show me a road;
If I encounter an enemy in war,
Give me six great hosts of troops.
I am cold; give me your coat.
If you are true, my father,
Give me your hand that scatters sustenance!'
The sacred Gray Pouch-Belt,
Was it not left by Manas?
He lays it snugly round his neck.
Speaking in this way, Semetey
Pleads with the dervish.
Then the dervish stands and says:
'May I circle round you, my foal!
I shall not come to your home;
I shall not give you a good blessing.
The reason I will not give it is this:
You imprison wandering ascetics;
If a man is a dervish, you torment him;
You beat those who cannot get away;
If a man is a khoja, you thrash him;
My foal, you lock him in his mosque.
If by chance, my foal,
Your anger rises fiercely,
You will beat me along with them.
One of the seven days is death;
My foal, one day at last you will die.
On the coming Day of Judgment,
Before the Prophet,
What answer will you give?'
When he spoke in this way,
Semetey stood and said:
'A playful child, when drunk,
When young and riding a stick,
Who does not beat, who does not strike?
When drunk from drinking spirits,
When young and dull of understanding,
Who does not thrash, who does not hit?
Who does not commit mischief?
I have left childhood behind;
I have begun the game anew.
I have kept a court and become a khan;
I have become a man of standing.
Now, father, may I fail to prosper if I touch a khoja;
If I molest a wandering ascetic,
May I cease to be a Muslim!
I shall not beat wandering ascetics;
I shall not imprison khojas.
Father, recognize that I am a child;
For now I give you this blue cloak.
Give your prayer and wear it as you go!
Father, if you enjoy the use of the cloak,
May you give me a blessing without measure.'
The blue cloak upon his shoulders,
To that poor dervish
He now took off and gave.
Truly created by God—
Did you see that he was His servant?
Of poor, solitary Manas—
Did you see that he was the son?
That the boy was a prince,
The dervish now knew.
The cloak from his shoulders,
Given to him for now, he put on.
Turning his face toward the qibla,
The white-bearded dervish
Raised his hands, saying, 'Allah!'
He now turned the bull's head.
He was no dervish, but Kyzyr;
He now stood and gave his blessing:
'Amen! Boy, spread your hands.
Your remotest ancestors were all khans;
Kyzyr has blessed you from your roots.
Your earliest forefathers were all khans,
Blessed by Kyzyr from the beginning,
Descendants of saints.
A star from heaven is my guiding sign;
When you attack the enemy with a shout,
May the Hungry Lion be your companion.
Your protector Kozhosan,
May he be your companion too.
At your right, the Forty Chiltens;
May a black-spotted leopard
Rage beside your flank.
May the Short-Tailed, Wolf-Maned Lion
Make ready close beside you.
May God open your road!
Amen! My son, have trust!
Raise your hands now.
Your descent is from forty maidens,
From the saint Mansur.
Your forefathers since that time—
I shall unfold them and tell you;
Without leaving a single one out,
I shall tell you with knowledge.
Your earliest forefather was Tumonkan,
Who made many raids through the night.
After him came Sanchykan,
Whose coming struck souls from bodies,
Whose voice drew blood,
Never sated by what he begged to drink,
Never giving up his greed.
Then came your forefather Akzholtoi,
And after him Sankoldoi.
From the two, Egidei and Sheyren,
After them came Khan Boyon;
From Khan Boyon came Khan Chayan;
From Khan Chayan came Balakan;
Descended from Balakan,
Karakan rose as a hero.
For the Muslims, few as a palmful,
They stood as a source of strength.
He too fought the Chinese for forty days.
From Karakan came Khan Jakyp;
From the dark, wolf-maned hero
Semetey was born in secret.
May God set your footsteps right;
May the lions of old support you!
May what you wear be bulletproof;
My foal, may your knowledge be surpassing!'
Having given his blessing,
The dervish standing there
Vanished from sight.
The cloak the boy had just given him
Was still upon the boy's back.
He was venerable, he was a sun;
The man who had given his blessing
Was Kyzyr himself.
When he looked, he could not see him;
The dervish who had blessed him—
Where he was could not be known.
The boy wandered, unable to ride on;
At the dervish's blessing,
He stared in dumbfounded wonder:
'What is this? The dervish
Began with an entirely different tale.
Ismail and Shaatemir—
These two were my fathers.
Where has he left them out?
I shall imprison wandering ascetics;
Dervishes such as this,
For their madness I shall beat.'
Speaking these words in this way,
He now rode along Ak-Chii's edge;
Zheti-Moinok and four ridges,
These the boy crossed.
Following the narrow street,
Your wolf-maned hero entered Bukhara.
He now raised a great commotion;
At one thing his sister had said earlier,
His heart now burned.
Into Temir Khan's treasury
He now made his way.
Temir Khan's Akbaran
He now snatched from the throne.
Ammunition in a white saddlebag
He now lifted onto the horse.
Temir Khan's Zulpukor
He slung on, scabbard and all.
Hurrying and hastening, Semetey
Ran to Aktulpar;
Across the steed's side,
He leaped up like a sheep and mounted.
The golden-cheeked battle-axe
Was looped about his wrist;
